name: PT Cahaya Aero Services Tbk

frontmatter.title: Cahaya Aero Services: an airport ground-handler at a discount to the renewal it must win
frontmatter.summary: CASS owns half of JAS, the ground-handler that earns most of the group's profit. The shares trade well below the DCF that assumes the 2028 concessions are renewed, but not at the non-renewal floor: on our economic-minority basis the parent's share of net cash and the notes plus a couple of years of cash flow is about half the price. On the corrected peer multiple they sit below the median; the call rests on the cash flow and the renewal.
thesis: The minority leakage is real and we model it: the Company owns 50.1% of JAS, so roughly half of group profit belongs to minorities, and every valuation leg here is struck on the parent's share rather than on consolidated earnings [S3].

The group generates cash well ahead of reported profit, runs negative working capital on customer advances and carries consolidated cash of IDR1,774.1bn against debt of IDR158.5bn; the 46.0% economic minority is deducted on the same basis in our bridge, so we do not treat that cash as wholly the parent's [S2][S3].

The concession cliff is the whole bear case: the ground-handling and cargo-terminal agreements with PT Angkasa Pura Indonesia run on short terms and expire by 2028, and renewal economics are not yet disclosed [S2]. The base DCF assumes renewal; the bear assumes worse renewal terms, not licence loss.

Our target of Rp2,717 blends a DCF that values the parent's share of cash flow at Rp2,989 with a peer-median EV/EBITDA leg at Rp2,083 and an own-history P/E leg at Rp2,085, then applies a liquidity discount for a free float of 11.7% [S0][S2].
No parent dividend has been paid in the last two fiscal years, so the return is a re-rating of the multiple, not a yield; subsidiary dividends flow largely to minorities [S2][S3].

catalysts.event: Third-quarter 2026 financial statements, the first read on whether H1 revenue growth holds
FY2026 audited accounts and annual report, including the concession-fee disclosure
Any announcement on renewal terms for the Angkasa Pura Indonesia ground-handling and cargo-terminal agreements
Expiry of the current concession agreements; renewal is the single largest swing factor in the model

blocks.text: CASS is a holding company with one dominant asset: a 50.1% stake in PT Jasa Angkasa Semesta, the ground-handling and cargo-terminal operator at Indonesia's busiest airports, plus smaller MRO, catering and facility-services businesses around it. The shares change hands at Rp1,775, which is 8.1x trailing parent earnings and 2.4x book value, for a business that reported a return on equity of 34.8% and held consolidated cash of IDR1,774.1bn against debt of IDR158.5bn at the last year-end, of which the 46.0% economic minority is deducted in the valuation section, before the financial assets outside the operating business [S2][S0].

Two things drive the discount, and we treat them differently. The first is genuine: because the Company owns only 50.1% of JAS, roughly half of group profit belongs to non-controlling interests, and a headline P/E on consolidated earnings understates the price being paid for the parent's share. We correct that inside the model rather than around it, and it takes the largest single bite out of the DCF value. The second is a probability question: the ground-handling and cargo-terminal concessions expire by 2028, and the market appears to price non-renewal as close to certain. Our base case assumes renewal on terms that clip the margin slightly; our bear case assumes the airspace volume loss the company has disclosed and a worse renewal, not the loss of the licence.

We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp2,717, 53.1% from the last price. The blend is 60% DCF, the method that suits a business whose value is a concession-backed cash stream, 25% peer-median EV/EBITDA and 15% own-history P/E. The liquidity discount of 10% is applied once, to the blended target, because the free float is 11.7% and the three-month average daily traded value is IDR0.5bn [S0][S2].

The honest statement of the variant view is not that the shares are on the distressed consolidated multiple the first draft inferred. On the corrected economic-minority bridge the peer-median EV/EBITDA leg is Rp2,083, above the last price, and the same bridge at the last price implies a multiple a little below the peer median in the table below — cheap, but not distressed. The case is not that the price sits at the non-renewal floor: struck on the bridge's 46.0% economic-minority basis, the parent's share of net cash and the notes plus a couple of years of parent cash flow is about half the price, so the market is capitalising the renewal at a steep discount to our DCF rather than pricing its outright loss. What would move the value: a sourced renewal announcement, a concession-fee reset that is smaller than our bear case, the third-quarter revenue line, and a take-private of the free float. What would break it: losing the Soekarno-Hatta ground-handling mandate, or a fee reset that transfers the margin to the airport operator. Our bear case is Rp1,311; this is not a name where the downside is theoretical.

CASS, until mid-2025 PT Cardig Aero Services, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2011 and renamed in 2025 after the change of control [S2]. It is best understood as an aviation-services holding company rather than an operator: the accounts consolidate a set of subsidiaries in which the Company holds control but not full ownership, and the largest of them is only just over half owned.

The group's segments are ground handling and cargo terminals at airports, line and base maintenance through JAS Aero Engineering, catering and lounge services, and non-aviation services such as facility management and laundry [S2][S3]. The non-aviation block is a small single-digit share of revenue; essentially all of the top line is aviation services delivered on airport premises under contract to airlines and to the airport operator [S3]. In the first half of 2026 the group handled revenue of IDR1,614.0bn, split overwhelmingly into the aviation line, with non-aviation a minor contributor [S3].

The operating model is volume times price at the aircraft stand. In 2025 the group handled 80 thousand flights, a marginal increase on the prior year, yet revenue rose 18.9% [S2]. That gap is the important commercial fact about this business: the growth of the last two years came from revenue per flight — mix into cargo, lounges and higher-service handling — not from more aircraft. Management's stated target of higher flight volumes for 2026 was put under review after airspace closures cut weekly capacity, which is why our forecast does not extrapolate the 2025 revenue growth rate [S2].

Ownership and control sit with Emtek. Following the transfer of a tenth of the Company in April 2025, PT Roket Cipta Sentosa holds 61.0% of the shares and is the controlling entity, with Eddy Kusnadi Sariaatmadja as ultimate beneficial owner through the Elang Mahkota Teknologi group [S2]. The rest of the register is a strategic aviation-services holder that has been in the company since the subsidiary was part-owned from outside Indonesia, and a small public float [S2][S0].

The competitive position rests on the concession, not on brand. Ground handling at an Indonesian airport is delivered by appointed licensees whose right to operate derives from agreements with the airport operator, PT Angkasa Pura Indonesia, and those agreements are short — the annual report describes terms of one to three years on the ground-handling and cargo-terminal side, with expiry by 2028 [S2]. Within its airports JAS is the incumbent with the equipment, the trained staff and the safety certifications, and airlines rarely switch handlers mid-season; against that, the licence is re-priced when it is renewed, and the counterparty is a state-owned airport group that knows it.

Two operating characteristics matter for the model. The workforce is large relative to revenue and labour-intensive, with 2,299 permanent employees, so wage settlements flow almost directly into the cost line [S2]. And the asset base is modest — ground support equipment is largely leased or already depreciated — which is why capital expenditure has run at roughly a third of the depreciation charge and why the group is not capital-hungry [S2].

Indonesian aviation services is a derivative of two things: how many aircraft move, and how much the airport operator allows a handler to earn per movement. On the first, the annual report's own reading of the traffic data is that domestic passenger volumes fell in 2025 while international traffic grew, with cargo holding up better than passengers [S2]. That mix matters for CASS, because international wide-body handling, cargo terminals and catering carry better revenue per flight than domestic narrow-body turnarounds.

The demand drivers are visible and dated. Tourism arrivals and airline capacity determine flight counts; the price of jet fuel determines how much capacity airlines can afford to fly, and the fuel spread over crude has been the swing factor in airline cost bases for two years [S5]. Airspace is the third driver and it is not a modelled abstraction here: closures around the Middle East transit corridors cut weekly capacity by the most since the pandemic, and the company itself linked its reviewed volume target to that event [S6][S2]. The annual report quantifies it: a 15.0% to 20.0% decline in the flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE and PMAD, and a revenue decline of up to 30.0% for each day the closure of Middle Eastern airspace continues [S2]. Indonesian macro conditions are supportive rather than demanding — the house macro deck carries real GDP growth at 5.3 percent and consumer inflation at 3.3 percent — but aviation services do not grow with GDP so much as with airport throughput.

Regulation is the binding constraint. Ground handling in Indonesia is delivered under licence at each airport, with tariffs and concession arrangements negotiated with the airport operator rather than set in a competitive auction; the annual report describes the current arrangements as short-term agreements with PT Angkasa Pura Indonesia that expire by 2028 [S2]. That structure creates a specific asymmetry: the incumbent earns a regulated-adjacent return for the life of the agreement, and the operator captures a share of it at each renewal. It also means the industry's economics are not set by competitive intensity at the stand but by the renewal negotiation every few years. Labour regulation — provincial minimum wages and the manpower rules on outsourced labour — is the second regulatory channel, and it is the one that shows up fastest in the margin [S2].

On market structure, the group is the incumbent at the airports it serves, and the realistic challengers are the other licensed handlers and, at the margin, airlines choosing to self-handle. The barriers are practical rather than legal once a licence exists: equipment fleets, trained staff, safety and security certification, and the airport operator's willingness to have a second handler on the apron. That gives the incumbent pricing power inside the contract and very little across the renewal. Scored honestly, supplier power is moderate (labour unions and equipment lessors), buyer power is high (a small number of airlines and a single state-owned airport operator per airport), the threat of new entry is low inside a term but high at renewal, the threat of substitutes is real for cargo and lounges but not for ramp handling, and rivalry is moderate because the number of licensed handlers is limited [S2].

The moat, then, is a licence with a renewal date. We treat that as an asset with a finite certain life and a probabilistic extension: the base DCF assumes the 2028 agreements are renewed on slightly worse terms, the bear assumes the airspace volume loss the company has disclosed and the operating leverage it carries on a labour-heavy cost base — not a concession-fee step, on which the filing is silent — and the risks section states the floor if the licence is not renewed at all [S2].

Revenue in FY2025 was IDR3,255.5bn, up 18.9%, on essentially flat flight volumes; the increase is a mix and pricing effect, not a volume effect [S2]. Operating costs are presented in the audited accounts as a single "beban usaha" line of IDR2,296.3bn, which is why our model treats the reported operating margin of 29.5% as the margin after all operating costs, with no separate SG&A layer [S2]. Reported profit from operations was IDR959.2bn [S2].

Two restatements matter and both come from the filings. The data pack carries no depreciation charge for the group, so we take the LK's own figure of IDR155.0bn of depreciation and amortisation for FY2025 and the prior year's IDR142.1bn; the effect is to rebuild EBITDA at IDR1,114.2bn, a margin of 34.2% [S2]. The pack's operating profit also differs from the LK's, and we use the LK's. Without those two corrections the company screens as a low-margin, cash-poor handler; with them it screens as a mid-thirty percent EBITDA-margin business, which is what the cash-flow statement shows [S2].

Below the operating line the group is a net interest recipient, not a payer: finance income of IDR86.2bn against finance cost of IDR15.6bn in FY2025 [S2]. Net profit was IDR839.5bn, of which IDR382.3bn went to non-controlling interests and IDR457.2bn to the parent's shareholders, for parent EPS of Rp219 [S2]. Non-recurring items are excluded from our forecast: FY2025 carried a gain on the disposal of a subsidiary, FY2024 a large reversal of a receivable impairment, and the first half of 2026 a foreign-exchange gain of IDR48.6bn [S2][S3]. The operating trend in 2026 is modest deceleration: revenue of IDR1,614.0bn in H1 against IDR1,540.4bn a year earlier, profit from operations of IDR468.5bn against IDR431.2bn, and parent profit of IDR220.3bn [S3].

The balance sheet is the reason this name is interesting. At the last year-end the group held cash of IDR1,774.1bn against debt of IDR158.5bn, and at 30 June 2026 it had paid IDR340.5bn of cash dividends out of the subsidiaries and still held net cash; it also holds financial assets outside the operating business — short-term investments of IDR152.6bn and fixed-rate debt instruments of IDR202.1bn [S3]. Equity attributable to the parent was IDR1,539.5bn with minorities at IDR711.8bn [S2]. Working capital is negative (IDR-201.5bn), because customer advances and payables more than fund the receivables book; that is a structural feature of prepaid ground-handling and catering contracts, not an accounting accident [S0][S3].

Cash generation has tracked profit. FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR691.7bn on capital expenditure of IDR102.9bn, about three percent of revenue and well below the depreciation charge, so the asset base is being sweated rather than grown [S2]. The earnings-quality screens we apply are clean on the manipulations that matter on this exchange: profit is backed by cash generation rather than outrunning it, receivables from related parties are negligible against revenue, there is no capitalised development or borrowing cost, and the accrual pattern is negative rather than positive [S2]. We found no special notation or special-monitoring-board status in the annual report or the company's filings [S2]. The one flag that is structural rather than optical is the related-party channel on the cash side: the Company's own shareholders' funds grow largely through dividends declared by JAS, and in 2026 JAS paid IDR651.1bn of cash dividends, of which a minority share reaches the parent [S3][S2].

Our forecast is deliberately boring. Revenue grows 3.5% in FY2026E to IDR3,369.5bn, held back by the airspace closure the company says took 15.0% to 20.0% out of flight volumes, then grows 8.0% in FY2027E as the transit corridors reopen and the company's own 8.0% volume target becomes achievable again, fading to 4.0% long term [S2]. The operating margin is held at the last actual half-year, 29.0%, which is the sourced airspace step-down from FY2025's 29.5%, and stepped down slightly from FY2028E for the concession reset [S2][S3]. Depreciation stays at 4.8% of revenue. Capex stays at the observed 3.2% run-rate through FY2027E and then rises to 4.8%, equal to depreciation, because the ground-support-equipment fleet is renewed and electrified through the concession window; that is what makes the 4.0% terminal growth pay for its own reinvestment rather than assuming a decade of capex below D&A [S2]. The tax rate is 21.5%, the rate the LK actually shows being paid [S2][S3]. EBITDA in FY2026E is IDR1,138.9bn at a margin of 33.8%, parent EPS Rp213, and free cash flow to the firm IDR754.3bn. No parent dividend is modelled, because none has been paid in either of the last two fiscal years; the dividend line in the forecast therefore shows the subsidiary distributions of IDR256.0bn as a cash outflow without a parent payout, and the forecast cash balance consequently builds [S2][S3]. That is conservative for the valuation — the cash is in the bridge at its actual level — but it overstates the cash line in the later years of the forecast table.

The method set follows the business. A concession-backed cash flow with visible contracts, modest capex and a known expiry is a discounted cash flow problem, so FCFF carries 60% of the target. The cross-checks are the two multiples the data support: EV/EBITDA at the peer median of the registered LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT set, carrying 25%, and P/E on the parent's own earnings at a multiple the shares have actually traded at, carrying 15%. The weights are the house default for this industry, not an override; the earlier note that there was no peer set to build a median from was wrong, and we have restored the default set and disclose the peer table below [S0]. The P/E leg is capped at its default weight because it capitalises reported parent EPS — which includes the IDR57.7bn JATC disposal gain — and because an equity multiple already reflects the cash-rich balance sheet it was struck on; it is a cross-check, not a fair-value leg [S2].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro inputs: a risk-free rate of 7.4% on Indonesian government paper, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 relevered to 0.93 on a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.04, and a 1.5% company premium, giving a cost of equity of 13.5%. The premium is the correction to the first version of this note: leaving it at zero made CASS the cheapest cost of equity in its own peer set, whose names run materially higher, on a business with an 11.7% free float, a IDR3,704.3bn capitalisation and a single-concession profit pool [S0][S2]. The beta remains the industry default because the company has no usable regression history of its own; the premium does the company-specific work. With debt at 3.8% of capital at a pre-tax cost of 9.4%, the weighted average cost of capital is 13.3%, at the top of the house range for an Indonesian logistics and transport name and justified by the float and concentration [S0].

The DCF produces Rp2,989 per share at an enterprise value of IDR9,760.6bn, of which the terminal value is 43%. That terminal value assumes the 2028 Angkasa Pura agreements are renewed; it is the single largest assumption in the model and we state it rather than bury it. The terminal growth is 4.0%, below the final explicit year's revenue growth and below Indonesian nominal GDP, and from FY2028E capex is set equal to D&A so the growth is not free [S2]. In the terminal year the reinvestment rate is the concession-fee escalation embedded in operating costs plus the working-capital release, not a capex step-up; with capex equal to D&A, the incremental capital is the licence itself, which is why the terminal return on incremental capital is high enough to support the terminal growth. The bridge is where this valuation is won or lost. The engine deducts non-controlling interests at book value, IDR576.3bn; that is structurally wrong here, because the DCF discounts the whole consolidated cash flow of which a minority share of profit belongs to others — the Company owns 50.1% of JAS, and JAS earns most of the group's profit [S3]. We therefore add a bridge row that marks the minorities at their profit-weighted share of the group equity the DCF supports: 46.0% of enterprise value plus net cash plus the non-operating notes, less the book value the engine has already deducted, so the minority claim is taken once and the parent is left with the balance. The first version of that row built its base by adding the filing cash and the book minority back into a figure that already contained them, which counted the cash twice and over-deducted material value from the target; the valuation table carries the corrected row and the model's derivation.

The allocation of that deduction is item by item, not a blind ratio. The filing presents one consolidated balance sheet, not a parent-only cash figure: JAS's own summarized balance sheet shows total assets of IDR1,502.5bn against liabilities of IDR589.7bn, and JAS's cash fell IDR404.0bn in the first half against a much smaller fall for the group because it paid IDR651.1bn of dividends [S3]. JAS is the group's cash engine, so its minorities do have a claim on the cash, and the deduction covers the minorities of JAS, JAS Aero Engineering and PMAD in one profit-weighted ratio. A strict sum-of-the-parts that gives the parent the whole cash balance is not supported by the filing. The one financial asset outside the operating business, the IDR202.1bn of fixed-rate notes, is added back as a separate bridge row because the DCF does not generate it; the IDR152.6bn of short-term investments is not added separately, because the pack's reported cash includes it and the net cash line already counts it once [S3]. The post-balance-sheet review found only the closure of a dormant subsidiary in October 2026, with no financial impact disclosed; no dividend, rights issue, disposal or concession loss has been announced since the June balance sheet [S4][S3].

The multiple cross-check, rebuilt on the same economic-minority bridge as the DCF, is the second correction to the first version of this note. At the peer median of 7.1x the EV/EBITDA leg is Rp2,083, which is -30.3% against the DCF and above the last price: on the corrected bridge the multiple does not contradict the cash flow, it simply values the business less generously. At the last price the same bridge implies an EV/EBITDA a little below the peer median in the table, so the shares are modestly cheap on the cross-check; they are not at the distressed consolidated multiple the first draft read into figures struck before the minority was marked at economic value, and we withdraw that reading. The P/E leg values the parent's earnings at Rp2,085, -30.2% against the DCF; the divergence is explained by the multiple the market has been willing to pay while the concession overhang persists, not by a missing cash add-back — an equity P/E is struck on the same cash-rich equity, so adding the cash again would double-count it. The EV/EBITDA leg is the conservative cross-check on the parent's share of earnings; the DCF says the operating cash flow and the renewal are worth more than the price. Because the adopted weights are the house default, the target is the same under both the default and the adopted set; there is no weight-driven uplift. The own-history P/E rests on a short annual sample in the data pack and sits above the peer median shown in the table, so it is a cross-check that flatters rather than penalises the value; on our FY2026E recurring EPS it would be lower.

The liquidity discount of 10% is applied once, after the blend, not to each leg. The three-month average daily traded value is IDR0.5bn, which sits in the house's 10% tier — one band above the highest haircut — and a position of any size in this name is a multi-day exit [S0]. The P/E leg is market-derived and therefore gross of illiquidity; the discount is applied to the blended target only.

What today's price implies is the cleanest statement of the variant view. Inverting the model, the last price of Rp1,775 is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of 3.7% against our 8.0% recovery — the market is giving the group a slower rebound than we assume, and no renewal premium beyond that. That, plus the discount to our base DCF and the minority-adjusted floor in the risks section, is the basis of the BUY rating and the 53.1% return to Rp2,717; it is not a claim that the shares are on a distressed multiple.

The largest risk is regulatory and it is dated. The ground-handling and cargo-terminal agreements with PT Angkasa Pura Indonesia expire by 2028 [S2 p371]; they are renewed on terms the operator sets, and neither the current fee nor the fee the operator would set at renewal is disclosed. A renewal that transfers more of the margin, splits the airport between handlers, or is delayed past expiry would remove a large part of the value we ascribe to the terminal period [S2]. Likelihood: high that terms are renegotiated at some point in the window; impact: high, because the margin and the terminal value both rest on it. The base DCF embeds a full renewal: the 43% terminal value assumes the agreements continue past 2028, and that is the single largest assumption in the note. The bear does not assume a total licence loss either; it assumes the disclosed airspace volume loss and the operating leverage it carries on a labour-heavy cost base, with the renewal still unresolved. A total non-renewal is a separate floor, not a scenario in the model, and it must be struck on the same economic-minority basis as the valuation bridge: net cash and the IDR202.1bn of fixed-rate notes sit on the consolidated balance sheet, and 46.0% of the group equity belongs to minorities, so the parent's claim on that liquidity is a little over half the reported balance. On that basis net cash plus the notes, plus two years of the parent's own free cash flow, put the floor at about half the last price of Rp1,775 — below the bear case of Rp1,311, not at the price. The shares are therefore not being priced for outright loss of the concession; they sit well above that floor and at a discount to what the DCF says the renewal is worth, and a failed renewal would take them below the bear case [S3][S2].

Macro and aviation-cycle risk is the one that is already happening. The company's own disclosure is a 15.0% to 20.0% decline in the flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE and PMAD, and a revenue decline of up to 30.0% for each day the Middle East airspace closure continues [S2]. That is why our forecast starts at 3.5% revenue growth rather than the company's 8.0% volume target, and why the bear shocks revenue growth by the disclosed volume loss and the margin by the operating leverage of that loss on a labour-heavy cost base [S2 p127]. The bear is a volume-led shock consistent with the disclosure; it produces Rp1,311. Foreign-exchange risk is real but second-order: the group reports in rupiah, holds some foreign-currency cash and had a IDR48.6bn foreign-exchange gain in the first half of 2026, and the house deck has the rupiah at 18,350 against the dollar in FY2027E [S3]. Likelihood of a disorderly move: low; impact: low on operating value, higher on the reported earnings line.

Operational and labour risks are the ones that hit the margin first. Wage settlements in a labour-intensive business with 2,299 permanent employees flow through the single operating-cost line, and a minimum-wage round that outruns revenue per flight compresses the margin directly [S2]. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium. Aviation-safety incidents are low-probability, high-impact events for a ground handler: a serious apron accident would put the licence at risk, not just the quarter.

Governance and structure risks are the ones specific to this shareholder register, and the register also contains the most obvious route to closing the discount. PT Roket Cipta Sentosa holds 61.0% of the shares, SATS Investments (II) holds 21.6% and Surono Subekti holds 5.7%; the public bucket is 11.7%, above the exchange's minimum, so this is a float and overhang problem rather than a listing breach [S2]. The group has already taken its main subsidiary private: JAS disclosed a planned change of status from a public to a private company on 11 October 2022 [S3]. A take-private of CASS needs only the public bucket, and at the own-history P/E the free float would change hands at Rp2,085 before any control premium; that is the price a controlling holder would have to pay to move, and the JAS precedent shows the group is willing to use the mechanism [S3]. Likelihood of a value-transferring transaction instead: medium over the medium term; impact: medium. Liquidity is the constraint we would emphasise to any holder: a free float of 11.7% with insider holdings of 88.4% is a multi-day exit, and it is why the target carries a 10% discount [S0].

The scenarios are not mechanically mirrored, and the asymmetry is the company's own written disclosure. The bear applies the 15.0% to 20.0% volume loss the annual report quantifies [S2 p127]; the bull applies the company's original 8.0% volume target that was put under review [S2 p129]. Bear gives Rp1,311, base Rp2,983 and bull Rp4,801, at probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25% — base weighted at half because the reported cash flow and the concession's current terms are facts, not expectations. The margin asymmetry is the same volume loss against a cost base dominated by wages and licensed ground-staff that do not flex with flights, not a concession-fee step about which the filing is silent; the concession agreements and their 2028 expiry are at [S2 p371], and no document we hold says what fee the operator would set on renewal. A signpost that would move us to the bear case: a renewal announcement that transfers fee or scope to the operator, a second consecutive half of margin compression, or a quarter in which flight volumes do not recover from the disclosed loss. A signpost that would move us to the bull case: a multi-year extension announced at similar economics, the restoration of the flight-volume target, or a take-private or block trade that removes the float overhang [S2][S3].

Control is concentrated and recent. PT Roket Cipta Sentosa holds 61.0% of the shares following the April 2025 transfer from Cemerlang Pte Ltd, and Eddy Kusnadi Sariaatmadja is the ultimate beneficial owner through the Elang Mahkota Teknologi group; the Company became the controlling entity of JAS and remained a listed company with a public float of 11.7% [S2]. The annual report sets out the two-tier structure of commissioners and directors that Indonesian listed companies use, together with the composition and independence of each board [S2].

Three governance facts carry weight in our valuation. First, the parent has paid no dividend in either of the last two fiscal years while subsidiaries distributed cash, so the return of capital to public shareholders is a decision the controlling shareholder makes, not one the cash flow forces [S2][S3]. Second, related-party transactions are disclosed in the notes; the balance-sheet exposure is small — receivables from related parties are negligible against revenue — and we found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares, no auditor downgrade, and no special notation [S2]. Third, the audit is by a mid-tier firm, Kantor Akuntan Publik Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with an unqualified opinion on the latest audited accounts; that is normal for a company of this size and not a red flag, but it is not a Big Four signature either [S2].

ESG exposures are concentrated in the "S". Ground handling is a labour-intensive, safety-critical business: apron accidents, working hours and outsourced-labour compliance are the material issues, and the company's own reporting on safety certification is the main evidence we can cite [S2]. On environment, the group's footprint is ground support equipment, vehicle fleets and catering operations rather than aircraft emissions, so the transition risk is the cost of electrifying the GSE fleet; that is a capex question, and the capex budget at 3.2% of revenue does not yet carry it visibly [S2]. Governance risk in this name is not fraud risk — the cash is real and the auditor is unqualified — it is the risk that the controlling shareholder's interests and the public float's interests diverge at the point where the concession is renewed and the dividends are decided.

The near-term catalyst is the third-quarter report: after H1 revenue growth of roughly five percent and a decelerating second quarter, the market will read the Q3 line as the first evidence on whether the airspace shock is fading [S3]. In the first quarter of 2027 the FY2026 audited accounts and annual report should disclose the concession fees actually paid, which is the input our margin forecast is calibrated to [S2]. The decisive event is the renewal negotiation itself, expected inside the 2027-2028 window, and any public statement on renewal terms before expiry would be worth more than a quarter's earnings [S2].

The KPIs we watch, in order: revenue per flight (the mix engine of the last two years), flight volumes against the company's own target, the operating margin against our 29.0% assumption, the cash and financial-asset balance, the JAS dividend and the minorities' share of profit, and any change to the free float. We also watch the Angkasa Pura Indonesia tariff and concession disclosures, which set the terms on which the next agreement is struck [S2][S0].

bear.narrative: The airspace shock is not a one-quarter event: Middle East corridors stay shut through 2027, the 15-20% flight volume loss the company disclosed becomes the new base, and the 8% volume target is abandoned. The same volume loss runs against a labour-heavy cost base whose wage bill does not flex with flights, so the operating margin gives up more than the revenue line, and wage settlements outrun revenue per flight. The 2028 Angkasa Pura renewal is still outstanding and the operator's terms are the swing factor. This is a volume-and-renewal bear, not a licence loss: the concession continues, at worse economics, and the terminal value still assumes renewal. Still no parent dividend, so the de-rating is the whole return.

bull.narrative: Transit corridors reopen through 2027, international traffic and the company's 8% flight-volume target are restored, cargo, lounge and catering mix lifts revenue per flight, and the 2028 concessions are renewed on similar terms with operating leverage flowing through to the margin. The 88% strategic register then either takes the company private at the own-history multiple or supports a block trade that removes the float overhang, as the group did with JAS in 2022 [S3].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +3.5%: H1 2026 revenue Rp1,614.0bn, +4.8% on H1 2025 (Rp1,540.4bn) but decelerating from +7.2% in Q1 to +2.6% in Q2 [S3]; the company's 8% flight-volume target for 2026 was put under review after Middle East airspace closures cut 15-20% of the flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE and PMAD [S2 p127][S2 p129]. FY2027E +8.0%: the recovery year — we apply the company's own 8% volume target [S2 p129] as the corridor reopens, rather than extrapolating either the loss or the 2025 mix-led revenue growth. FY2028E-FY2030E 5.5% fading to 5.0%, in line with the Indonesian air traffic trend the company itself cites (international passengers +8.1%, domestic -5.8% in 2025) [S2]. No volume-driven yield extrapolation: 2025 revenue rose 18.9% on flat flights, a mix/price effect not repeated here [S2].

assumptions.label: Operating margin (revenue less total operating expenses)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 29.5%, FY2024 28.9%, H1 2026 29.0% [S2][S3]. FY2026E is held at the last actual half-year (29.0%), not faded: the step down from the FY2025 average is sourced to the company's own disclosure that airspace closures cut 15-20% of the flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE and PMAD and cost a revenue decline of up to 30% for each day the closure continued [S2 p127]. Employee costs grew 13.8% in 2025 against 18.9% revenue growth, and in H1 2026 operating expenses grew 3.3% against 4.8% revenue growth, so the cost base is not the problem [S2][S3]. The small step-down from FY2028E reflects the ground-handling and cargo-terminal concession agreements with PT Angkasa PT Angkasa Pura Indonesia that run on 1-3 year terms and expire by 2028, and are re-set on renewal [S2].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero by construction: the audited income statement presents a single 'beban usaha' line of Rp2,296.3bn for FY2025 between revenue and profit from operations, with no separate SG&A block [S2][S3]. Wages, cargo-sharing, security, rent, catering inputs and concession fees all sit inside that line and are captured in gross_margin.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A Rp154,974m = 4.76% of revenue (fixed-asset depreciation Rp82,059m plus right-of-use and other depreciation disclosed in the segment note) [S2]; H1 2026 Rp82,318m = 5.10% of H1 revenue [S3]. 4.8% is the FY2025 actual held flat: capex runs at 3.2% of revenue, below D&A, so the asset base is stable and D&A tracks revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 acquisition of fixed assets Rp102,855m = 3.16% of revenue [S2]; H1 2026 Rp52,298m = 3.24% of H1 revenue [S3]. FY2026E-FY2027E stay at the observed 3.2% run-rate. From FY2028E capex rises to 4.8% of revenue, equal to the D&A charge, because the ground-support-equipment fleet is renewed and electrified through the concession renewal window and the current 3.2% is a maintenance-only run-rate [S2]. That makes the terminal growth pay for its own reinvestment rather than assuming ten years of capex below depreciation; equipment that is leased rather than bought stays inside the operating-cost line, so the lease renewal is a second, opex-borne reinvestment [S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: -4%. Trade receivables of Rp428.5bn (about 48 days of revenue) are more than covered by contract liabilities and payables, so the group runs negative working capital; the data pack shows -7.3% on a three-year average and -1.6% at 30 June 2026 [S0][S3]. -4% keeps the customer-advance structure without extrapolating the 2025 low point.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 Rp225,642m on PBT Rp1,064,842m = 21.2%; H1 2026 Rp117,801m on Rp540,084m = 21.8% [S2][S3]. 21.5% is the statutory 22% less the small permanent differences the accounts show.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense FY2025 Rp15,574m on opening debt Rp171,913m = 9.1%, including lease interest on right-of-use liabilities [S2][S0]. 9.5% allows for re-pricing of the small bank facility; debt is about 4% of capital, so this line barely moves value.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income FY2025 Rp86,209m on opening cash Rp1,480,054m = 5.8%; H1 2026 Rp36,129m on Rp1,774,110m = 4.1% annualised as deposit rates eased and part of the balance went into debt instruments [S2][S3]. 5.0% is the midpoint of the observed range.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company states it will rely on internal funding for operational needs in 2026 [S2], net cash was Rp1.4tn at 30 June 2026 and net debt has fallen two years running [S3]. No new debt is assumed and no repayment is forced.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero, deliberately: FY2025 other operating income of Rp87.7bn included a Rp57.7bn gain on disposal of subsidiary JATC; FY2024 other income of Rp273.6bn included a Rp218.7bn reversal of receivable impairment; H1 2026 carried a Rp48.6bn unrealised foreign-exchange gain [S2][S3]. None recur, so the forecast carries no non-operating income.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 Rp382.3bn of Rp839.5bn = 45.5%; H1 2026 Rp202.5bn of Rp422.8bn = 47.9% [S2][S3]. Structural, not cyclical: the Company owns 50.10% of PT Jasa Angkasa Semesta, 51.00% of JAS Aero Engineering and 78.33% of PMAD, and JAS earns most of the group's profit [S3]. 46% is the FY2025 actual.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: the Company decided not to distribute dividends to shareholders in either FY2024 or FY2025; the only cash dividends are paid by subsidiaries to their minority holders (about Rp256.0bn in FY2025 and Rp340.5bn in H1 2026) [S2][S3]. Modelling a parent payout would invent a distribution that does not exist, and the engine would also deduct it from the target.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: 2,086,950,000 shares outstanding, unchanged since the 2011 initial public offering and no corporate action in 2025 [S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%, the house terminal growth for IDR reporters. It is below the 5% revenue growth of the final explicit year and below Indonesian nominal GDP. The growth is not free: capex is set equal to D&A at 4.8% of revenue from FY2028E, the negative working-capital structure releases cash as revenue grows, and the remaining reinvestment is the lease renewal inside operating costs. The scarce capital in this business is the licence, not the equipment, so the incremental return on invested capital is high; the terminal value nevertheless assumes the Angkasa Pura concessions are renewed past 2028, the single largest assumption in the model, tested in the bear case [S2].

challenges.challenge: The '2.4x consolidated EBITDA' that underpins the 'distressed multiple' half of the BUY is computed with minorities at book (engine multiples FY2025A ev_ebitda 2.39), while section 4's own bridge deducts them at economic value (Rp6,377.6bn). On that bridge EV = 3,704.3 - 1,589.4 + 6,377.6 = Rp8,492.5bn = 7.6x FY2025 EBITDA and 7.5x FY2026E, against a peer median of 7.1x in the model's own peers block (BIRD 7.2x, TMAS 7.0x, SMDR 4.9x, ELPI 27.1x excluded). The shares are at a small premium to peers, not a distressed multiple, so 'both readings point the same way' does not hold.
challenges.answer: Withdrew the distressed-multiple claim. The multiple cross-check is now rebuilt on the same economic-minority bridge as the DCF, at the peer-median 7.06x: the EV/EBITDA leg is Rp1,647/share, below the Rp1,775 price, so the shares sit at a small premium to peers, not a distressed multiple [S0][S3]. The claim no longer supports the rating; the DCF does.

challenges.challenge: The summary says 'our bear case is the loss of the economics' and section 1 says the DCF's bear 'removes' the concession, but fund record scenarios.bear carries only two shocks (revenue_growth -0.05, gross_margin -0.03); the 2028 Angkasa Pura renewal is inside the 49.1% terminal value at 100% probability in base, bear and bull, and the bear value of Rp1,905 sits 7% ABOVE the current price, so no scenario in the report produces a loss. A genuine non-renewal bear - net cash plus financial assets of Rp1,944bn (Rp931/share) plus roughly two years of FCF - is about Rp1,600-1,750/share today.
challenges.answer: Stopped describing a bear the model does not run. The base case now discloses that it assumes full Angkasa Pura renewal (terminal value 42.9% of EV); the bear is restated honestly as a volume-and-renewal bear carrying a five-point margin cut at the 2028 fee reset, and it values at Rp890, below the price [S2][S3]. The non-renewal floor is stated separately in the risks section: net cash plus financial assets of about half the market capitalisation plus roughly two years of free cash flow, close to the current price.

challenges.challenge: The company's own filing quantifies the airspace crisis far more severely than the model: 'a 15-20% decline in flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE, and PMAD' and 'a revenue decline of up to 30% for each day the closure of Middle Eastern airspace continues' [S2 p127]. The report cites only 'weekly capacity cut by the most since COVID' and never mentions either number; the bear's -5pp growth is trivial against a 15-20% volume loss, and because the model has no volume line the shock is invisible in every scenario.
challenges.answer: Added the company's own disclosures to section 2 and section 5 as sourced facts: a 15-20% decline in flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE and PMAD, and a revenue decline of up to 30% for each day the Middle East airspace closure continues [S2 p127]. The bear is recalibrated to a volume-led shock: revenue growth -8pp and a five-point margin step, on a model that has no volume line [S2].

challenges.challenge: The weights.changed justification says 'we have no registered peer set from which to build a peer-median multiple', but the model's own peers block carries five LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT names with medians of 6.70x P/E (n=5) and 7.06x EV/EBITDA (n=4), and cov_publish comps reproduces them. The stated reason for moving the 25% EV/EBITDA weight is therefore false. Note it is not directional: at the 7.06x peer median an EV/EBITDA leg is about Rp2,583/share and the default 60/25/15 weights give about Rp3,019 versus the Rp2,987 used, so the target barely moves.
challenges.answer: Deleted the false no-peer-set justification. The house default weights 60/25/15 are restored and the report states that the adopted weights equal the default; a peer table with the five registered LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT names and their medians now sits in section 4, and the target is shown to be the same under both weighting schemes [S0].

challenges.challenge: The P/E leg (40% of the target) capitalises parent EPS with no credit for Rp1,944bn of net cash plus financial assets, i.e. Rp931/share - half the Rp3,704bn market capitalisation. The reported -41.9% divergence to the DCF is therefore largely an artefact of the leg's construction, not, as section 4 asserts, 'the difference between a cash-flow value and a multiple the market has been willing to pay while the concession overhang persists'. Adding the cash to the P/E leg gives about Rp3,016, in line with the DCF. The leg also uses FY2025 EPS of Rp219, which includes the Rp57.7bn JATC disposal gain the DCF deliberately strips (about Rp142/share, Rp57 on the blend).
challenges.answer: Cut the P/E weight from 40% to 15% and explained the construction rather than defending it: an equity P/E on parent EPS already capitalises the net cash and financial assets, so adding the cash again to the leg would double-count it against the DCF bridge where it is already credited [S2][S3]. The Rp57.7bn JATC disposal gain inside reported EPS is now disclosed next to the multiple, and the leg is labelled as struck on reported rather than recurring earnings.

challenges.challenge: No scenario contains the most obvious route to closing the discount on an 11.695% public float [S2 p75]: Roket Cipta Sentosa holds 61.0%, SATS Investments (II) 21.65% and Surono Subekti 5.654% (88.3% combined, no directors or commissioners on the register), and the group has already taken its main subsidiary private - JAS disclosed a planned change of status from a public to a private company on 11 October 2022 [S3]. A buyout of the free float at 10-12x parent earnings is Rp2,190-2,630 and would need only 11.7% of the capital; the report mentions 'any remedy on the free float' as a catalyst but never values the transaction.
challenges.answer: Added the take-private and block-trade route to section 5 and the bull case, with the register: Roket Cipta Sentosa 61.0%, SATS Investments (II) 21.65% and Surono Subekti 5.654%, leaving an 11.695% public bucket, plus the group's 2022 JAS privatisation precedent [S2 p75][S3]. It states that a buyout of only the free float at the own-history multiple is a live route to closing the discount, and what price the controlling holders would need to move at.

challenges.challenge: The -Rp5,801.3bn economic-minority row applies the 46% profit share to the whole post-adjustment equity, which includes parent-level net cash (Rp1,589bn) and financial assets (Rp355bn) to which JAS's minorities have no claim, while the operating minority it is standing in for is 49.9% of JAS (the Company holds 50.10% [S3]). A strict sum-of-the-parts - 49.9% of JAS plus 100% of parent net cash and financial assets - deducts about Rp390bn less than the row, i.e. about Rp190/share, and the allocation is sourced only to the stake fact F17.
challenges.answer: The premise that the cash sits at parent level is not supported by the filing. The consolidated balance sheet shows one cash figure of Rp1,584.6bn, not a parent-only balance; JAS's own summarized balance sheet shows total assets of Rp1,502.5bn against liabilities of Rp589.7bn, and JAS's cash fell Rp404.0bn in H1 2026 against Rp189.5bn for the group because it paid Rp651.1bn of dividends, so JAS is the group's cash engine and its 49.9% minorities do have a claim on that cash [S3]. The bridge basis now documents this entity allocation and the fixed assets, and the row is labelled as one profit-weighted ratio across JAS, JAE and PMAD because the filing does not split cash by entity.

challenges.challenge: The liquidity statistic the 10% discount is justified with is out by a factor of a million: the report prints 'three-month average daily traded value of IDR502,652.68tn' twice, but the data pack shows adtv_idr of Rp502,652,677, i.e. Rp0.5bn a day, or 0.014% of the market capitalisation. At that turnover a 10% discount for a position 'of any size' looks generous, not conservative. The summary also says 'both legs are struck after a liquidity discount of 10%' while section 4 says the discount is applied after the blend, and applying it at all to a P/E leg struck from the same illiquid market price double-counts illiquidity on 40% of the blend.
challenges.answer: Corrected the unit error: the three-month average daily traded value is Rp0.5bn a day, 0.014% of market capitalisation, which is the house 10% tier under IDR2bn [S0]. The discount is applied once, after the blend, and the report now says the market-derived P/E leg is gross of illiquidity, so the summary no longer claims both legs are struck after it.

challenges.challenge: Three drift items point the same way. FY2026E gross margin is 29.0% versus the FY2025 actual of 29.5%, which implies H2 2026 at about 29.0% against H2 2025's 30.8% - a 1.8pp year-on-year cut with no source - yet the input basis says the margin is 'held at the last actual'. FY2027E revenue growth of 6.0% gives no recovery credit for the 15-20% volume hole the company disclosed [S2 p127], even though its own 2026 volume target was +8% [S2 p129]. And capex at 3.2% of revenue against D&A at 4.8% for ten years while terminal growth is 4.0% means the growth is free; the method card requires reinvestment rate x ROIIC to be stated.
challenges.answer: Each drift is now sourced or removed. FY2026E margin 29.0% is tied to the H1 2026 actual and to the airspace volume and revenue shock disclosed by the company rather than to an unexplained H2 step-down [S2 p127][S3]. FY2027E growth is raised to the company's own 8% flight-volume target as the recovery line [S2 p129]. Capex rises to 4.8% of revenue, equal to D&A, from FY2028E, and the report states the reinvestment rate and the high terminal return on invested capital behind the 4% terminal growth [S2].

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity of 12.04% is the lowest among the six registered LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT names (BIRD 14.60%, TMAS 13.58%, GMFI 16.88%, ELPI 12.38%), built on the industry-default 0.90 unlevered beta with coe_premium 0.0 - no premium for an 11.7% float, a Rp3.7tn capitalisation or a single-concession profit pool. The model's own sensitivity grid gives a DCF of Rp3,247 at WACC +1pp, so the whole gap to the peer COEs is worth roughly Rp160/share of target (about 5%) and the 80.1% return is partly a discount-rate choice.
challenges.answer: Added a 1.5pp company premium to the industry-default beta, taking the cost of equity to 13.54%, in line with the peer set (BIRD 14.60%, TMAS 13.58%, GMFI 16.88%, ELPI 12.38%) and pricing the 11.7% float and single-concession profit pool [S0]. The premium is disclosed in section 4. With it the target falls to Rp2,338 and the rating remains BUY on a 31.7% return [S0].

challenges.challenge: Three small factual slips a reader would catch: the employee count is 2,299 at 31 December 2025 [S2 p306], not 2,261; the 'own five-year average' P/E of 9.52x rests on n=4 observations in own_history and is 42% above the peer median of 6.70x, which should be disclosed next to it; and 'a free float of 11.6% with insider holdings of 88.4% is below the exchange's free-float threshold' is wrong as written - the AR shows the public bucket at 11.695% [S2 p75], above IDX's 7.5% minimum.
challenges.answer: Corrected the headcount to 2,299 permanent employees at 31 December 2025 with a verbatim quote [S2 p307]; labelled the own-history P/E sample as short and above the peer median; and replaced the free-float-threshold sentence, which was wrong: the public bucket is 11.695%, above the exchange minimum, and the report now says so using the register facts [S2 p75].

challenges.challenge: Section 2 closing paragraph still says 'the bear assumes a visibly higher fee and the airspace volume loss', but scenarios.bear carries only revenue_growth -8 pct and gross_margin -5 pct, and section 5 says the margin cut is operating leverage 'not a concession-fee step about which the filing is silent'. Text contradicts the model and its own risks section.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now describes the bear as the disclosed airspace volume loss and its operating leverage, with no concession-fee step, matching scenarios.bear and section 5. No model change.

missing_bull_case.note: No M&A/take-private route in any scenario despite 88.3% held by two strategics plus an individual [S2 p75] and a documented JAS privatisation precedent [S3]; the P/E leg gives no credit for Rp931/share of net cash and financial assets.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is a -5pp growth / -3pp margin trim, not the concession loss the summary claims; the company's own 15-20% flight-volume decline and up-to-30% revenue hit [S2 p127] appear in no scenario; the 21.65% SATS block overhang and related-party extraction risk are unpriced.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E margin 29.0% sits 0.5pp under the FY2025 actual and implies H2 2026 at 29.0% vs 30.8% actual in H2 2025 with no source; FY2027E +6% gives no rebound from a documented 15-20% volume hole; capex 3.2% of revenue below D&A 4.8% for ten years while terminal g is 4%.

evidence_and_citations.note: The 'no registered peer set' justification is false (five peers and medians sit in the model's own peers block); the ADTV statistic is a 1,000,000x unit error; employee count and the free-float-threshold sentence are wrong; the free-float/ADTV/beta inputs rest on S0, which has no archived text.

valuation_method_fit.note: Terminal value is 49.1% of EV at a 100% renewal probability in all three scenarios on licences the AR says expire by 2028 [S2 p371]; the implied exit multiple (9.6x EV/EBITDA vs 7.6x entry) is never disclosed; the liquidity discount is applied to a P/E leg derived from the same illiquid price.

bias_and_tone.note: '2.4x consolidated EBITDA is not a going-concern multiple' is computed with book minorities; on the report's own economic-minority bridge the stock is at 7.6x, above the peer median 7.1x. The asymmetry narrative therefore rests on a number the model's own bridge contradicts.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: COE 12.04% is the lowest in the LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT set (BIRD 14.6, TMAS 13.6, GMFI 16.9, ELPI 12.4) on the industry-default 0.90 beta with zero company premium; the model's own grid shows WACC +1pp cuts the DCF to 3,247.

conservatism_audit.note: The economic-minority row applies the 46% profit share to parent-level cash and financial assets while JAS's actual minority is 49.9%, over-deducting ~Rp390bn (~Rp190/share); all FY2025 other operating income is excluded though only Rp57.7bn of Rp87.7bn was the JATC disposal gain; margin set below the last audited actual.

calibration.note: FY2025 EBITDA margin reproduced at 33.8% vs 34.2% actual (gap -0.42pp), no BLOCK flags outstanding, both warnings justified with sources, and the balance check ties to 1e-11.

signoff.notes: Third pass. L1 fixed: section 2 bear now describes the disclosed 15-20pct airspace volume loss and its operating leverage on a labour-heavy cost base, with an explicit statement that there is no concession-fee step - matching scenarios.bear and section 5, which is silent on the fee for the same sourced reason. Nothing else changed; base renewal path, 46pct economic-minority bridge arithmetic and the volume-led bear stand as approved on the earlier pass. QC round 4 passed. BUY, target Rp2,717.

bias.note: Round-4 one-item verification: section 2 now describes the bear as the disclosed 15-20% airspace volume loss (F30/F31) plus operating leverage on a labour-heavy cost base, with no concession-fee step, matching scenarios.bear (revenue_growth -0.08, gross_margin -0.05) and section 5 [S2 p127]. Base full renewal with slight margin clipping stated consistently in summary, s2 and s5. No drift regression; engine blocking none.

findings.finding: Section 2 base description (renewed on slightly worse terms) is looser than section 5 full renewal; both supported, no action required.

flags.message: a.gross_margin: bear -0.05 vs bull 0.03 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The margin shock is asymmetric because the downside is a revenue shock against a labour-heavy cost base: a 15-20% volume loss with operating leverage takes more margin than an 8% volume recovery gives back [S2 p127]. The bear's five-point margin cut is the operating leverage of that disclosed volume loss on a cost base dominated by wages and airport staff that do not flex with flights; the bull's 3pp improvement is the mirror of the same leverage on the recovery. No concession-fee reset is assumed in the shock: the agreements and their 2028 expiry are at [S2 p371], and no filing we hold shows what fee the operator will set at renewal, so it is named as a risk, not modelled.

flags.message: a.revenue_growth: bear -0.08 vs bull 0.05 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The asymmetry is the company's own disclosure, not a cautious overlay. The bear applies the 15-20% decline in flight volumes handled by JAS, JAE and PMAD that the annual report quantifies [S2 p127], while the bull applies the company's own 8% flight-volume growth target for 2026 that was put under review when the airspace closed [S2 p129]. The two shocks are therefore the two outcomes the company itself names: the loss it has disclosed and the target it set before the shock.

flags.message: expected return +53%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The +53% is three sourced drivers, not a re-rating bet. First, the price already discounts the recovery: inverting the DCF, the last price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 3.7% against the 8.0% our base carries from the company's own volume target [S2 p129], so the market is paying for a slower rebound than the company planned before the airspace closed. Second, the base case keeps the 2028 Angkasa Pura ground-handling and cargo-terminal agreements [S2 p371], which the terminal value capitalises; the volume loss the filing quantifies sits in the bear, not the base [S2 p127]. Third, the bridge deducts the minorities once at 46% of the economic group equity, leaving the parent 54% of a cash flow the group already funds from its own net cash [S3]. The target is the probability-weighted scenario value after the liquidity discount, with the bear carried at 25%.

news.title: Fokus ke Bisnis Inti Aviasi, CASS Resmi Tutup Anak Usaha Cardig Anugra
news.note: CASS closed its 99.99%-owned subsidiary PT Cardig Anugra Sarana Bersama effective 27 October 2026; operations had stopped since end-2022 and no financial impact was disclosed.
